messages.body_plain:
Hi Vincent,

Many thanks for the prompt reply. Your responses re points 2-4 all look great. I think the strategy==3 will work to get around the start time issues.

Re point 1 - the number of nights looks correct, and I believe the inactivity indicator looks ok, although I have nothing to compare it to. I've attached a screenshot of a fairly typical output in the PDF, the light blue line is largely up during the period I would expect sleep. I'm getting this error for multiple datasets. I tried processing 2-3 random files from multiple datasets, but I get the error in all cases.

It might be helpful to know that the "invalid factor level" error is generated during part 3 of the shell script. I assume that is what is invalidating the part 4 report?

Again, appreciate the help.

Many thanks,
Taren

On Monday, 1 August 2016 04:18:21 UTC+10, Vincent van Hees wrote:
> Hi Taren,
>
> 1. Can you inspect the pdfs that are generated and stored in subfolder meta/sleep.qc/... Do these make sense to you? For example, do you count the expected number of nights, and is the sustained inactivity indicator (bottom colored line) up when you would expect it? Secondly, can you check whether the error occurs for all your datasets and files or just for one specific file or dataset? If yes, try to verify what makes that dataset different.
>
> 2. If you always expect a specific number of days of measurement then you could try variable 'strategy =  3' with ndayswindow specified. I developed this for a study where they sent the accelerometer by mail to the participant without knowing exactly when the participant would start wearing the monitor. If that doesn't work for your study design then split your dataset in subsets such that each subset has more or less the same number of non-wear hours at the beginning of the measurement. Inspecting the pdf plots produced by part 2 may help you here. Next, process each subset with strategy =2 and hrs.del.start set specific to that subset.
>
> 3. See response by Stuart... also note that all the epoch by epoch values are stored in the RData milestone data. So, if you or someone around you is a bit familiar with R you can extract this information yourself. IMP$metashort as produced by part2 has all the epoch by epoch acceleration values.
>
> 4. To some extend the code facilitates sensitivity analyses to a variety of parameters, but I did not facilitate this for all parameters assuming that for most of them people do not even want to run sensitivity analyses. To do this there are currently two options: (1) Run the analyses multiple times with different parameter settings and make a copy of the intermediate outputs. (2) Make a copy of the entire output folder after you have run part1 and then run part 2, 3 and/or 4 for each copy of the output separately. To do this make sure that the various copies of the output folder have a name that starts with 'output_' followed by an informative description xx about what you intended to do with them. Next, set argument studyname to xx and make sure that xx matches the xx in "output_xx". Also, set argument datadir to c(). In that way the code will consider each copy of the output folder as a separate study, named xx.
>
> Vincent
>

messages.body_plain:
Hi Jairo,
In R you would do this as:
calibrated_acceleration = scale(acceleration,center = -offset, scale = 1/scale).

If you also want to use the temperature offset correction then the formula is:
calibrated_acceleration = scale(acceleration,center = -offset, scale =
1/scale) + scale(temperature, center = rep(meantempcal,3), scale =
1/tempoffset)

Note that meantempcal is the mean temperature of the data used for
deriving the calibration coefficients.

Best regards,
Vincent

messages.subject: GGIR 1.2-10 online
messages.body_plain:
GGIR version 1.2-10 is now online.

I have summarized the key updates here <https://cran.r-project.org/web/packages/GGIR/news.html>.

I felt the need to change the function argument for specifying bout calculation again. The underlying calculations are exactly the same though.

The original implementation from 2014 is still there (use bout.metric = 1 to get those). Earlier this year I thought the original 2014 implementation was inappropriate and so I added a new metric, being bout.metric 2. However, after thinking more about it I do not think that either one of them is truly superior; they are just different ways of quantifying a bout.

My impression is that there is not much literature on how to count a bout in the presence of epoch-level data with epoch lengths shorter than 1 minute. So, I implemented another metric (number 3) to allow myself to compare various options. I documented all three metrics and added function g.getbout. This function should enable the user to inspect my code for bout calculation, test it isolated from the rest of the package, and help identify what metric for calculating bouts is most sensible.

The challenge with designing a bout metric is that we need to decide how to account for breaks in bouts, how to account for the natural occurrence of values below or above a threshold because of the Gaussian nature of the data, and how to account for beliefs about what constitutes a physiologically meaningful bout of activity or inactivity: Do we allow someone to take a 10 second break? and how about a 1 minute break? Should the length of the maximum break length be proportional to the duration of the bout? Can there be activity bouts within a very long inactivity bout?

If anyone knows literature investigating this issue then I would appreciate hearing from you. If new bout metrics are to be added in the future then I will just number them 4, 5, ... So, in that way reproducibility of original calculations should be preserved regardless of whether we like them.

Thanks,

Vincent

messages.subject: Some questions about GGIR package
messages.body_plain:
Hi Vincent (and everyone),

First of all thank you for developing this fantastic package.

I have some doubts that I hope you can answer:

1- About device placement:  I believe that all algorithms (e.g. autocalibration, non-wear time and sleep time detection,...) implemented in GGIR have been developed for non-dominant wrist data, haven't it? If so, Could I expect a well-functioning of autocalibration (implemented with g.calibrate) for hip data? I think that non-wear detection and sleep algorithms are specific for device placement and they are not supposed to work well in hip for instance, have they been proved with hip data?

2- MVPA cut-points: I've seen that MVPA time detection is done through cut-points based on different metrics (most of them on ENMO). I think this method is similar to the one applied with counts, and then it can have the same limitations. What is your opinion about that? Do you trust in cut-point methods to detect MVPA or do you know other methods that have been tested?

3- Sedentary time: Is there any function in GGIR especialized in detecting sedentary time??

4- Sleep time: Could you explain how to enter a sleeplog manually? It have to be done file with the arguments sleeplog_onset and sleeplog_wake? or is ther any easier method? And another question, I have run g.part4 in my data without entering a sleeplog, however, in the data frame resulting from that function I have variables called "sleeplog_onset", "sleeplog_wake", etc. Where these values come from if I didn't enter any sleeplog?

Thanks again for your work!

Best regards,
Jairo Hidalgo Migueles

messages.subject: Re: [GGIR] Some questions about GGIR package
messages.body_plain:
Hi Jairo,
Good questions! I have inserted my answers in your email below.
Best, Vincent

On 31 August 2016 at 16:48, Jairo Hidalgo Migueles

<jairo.hidal...@gmail.com> wrote:
>
> 1- About device placement:  I believe that all algorithms (e.g. autocalibration, non-wear time and sleep time detection,...) implemented in GGIR have been developed for non-dominant wrist data, haven't it? If so, Could I expect a well-functioning of autocalibration (implemented with g.calibrate) for hip data? I think that non-wear detection and sleep algorithms are specific for device placement and they are not supposed to work well in hip for instance, have they been proved with hip data?

>>> Answer: None the calculations in GGIR is body location specific and I have tried to design GGIR in a way that it could work for any body location. You a correct though that most of the work to support GGIR is based on wrist data, by which it is possible that GGIR is better justified for wrist data than for other body locations. However, I have good hope for its generic use for the following reasons:
- The auto-calibration algorithm relies on having sufficient
calibration points around the sphere (as explained in the  2014
paper). This may easier with wrist data than with hip data, but the
good thing about function g.calibrate is that it also evaluates its
own performance and will tell you whether the autocalibration was
successful; see QC output in GGIR. My experience is that the algorithm
works fine for hip data, but as I said you will always be able to
verify this yourself if in doubt.
- Non-wear detection is by its own definition not body location
specific. The algorithm is based on the signal noise level over large
time windows, by default 1 hour. Therefore, I see no reason to doubt
the performance of the non-wear detection for studies with different
sensor attachment locations because we make all kinds of tiny
movements with our body parts, which will trigger the wear-detection
as soon as there is more variance in the data than would be expected
from sensor noise. If you are in doubt then just do some experiments
on yourself to see how GGIR handles an inactive day in the office or
an evening behind the television and then investigate whether the code
detects all your inactivity correctly as monitor-wear time.
- The sleep detection algorithm is essentially a description of the
data, as in: did the accelerometer orientation change by more than A
degrees over a time window of B minutes. In my opinion there is
nothing body location specific about that. Only when the
wrist-specific parameters (5 degrees and 5 minutes) which I evaluated
in last year’s paper are entered then the sleep detection will become
wrist specific. So, in other words: A new set of parameters may make
the algorithm equally well suitable for any other body location. All
you need is a dataset to demonstrate that your new parameters are
plausible for your new sensor location.

2- MVPA cut-points: I've seen that MVPA time detection is done through
cut-points based on different metrics (most of them on ENMO). I think
this method is similar to the one applied with counts, and then it can
have the same limitations. What is your opinion about that? Do you
trust in cut-point methods to detect MVPA or do you know other methods
that have been tested?

>>> Answer: I am aware of the limitations of cut-points. I do not think that there is a convincing alternative approach available. Cut-points are easy to replicate which is good for methodological consistency, and easy to evaluate and update even by non-technical users. The relationship between acceleration and human energy expenditure is complex. Within single activity types the relationship between acceleration and energy expenditure may seem fairly linear. However, the linear relationship has a different slope and y-intercept between activity types (see my 2009 publication in Obesity), and those differences between activity types are in turn also dependent on body weight and age of the person being measured. So, if we consider real life conditions with a variety of activity types and a variety of individuals then the relationship between acceleration and energy expenditure is highly non-linear. One of the key problems in dealing with this non-linearity is that a substantial part of the non-linearity is actually caused by the energy expenditure construct itself and not by the limitations of the accelerometer. For example, MET values for the activity type sitting differ hugely between lean and overweight individuals, while the entire PA research community assumes that MET values are constant per activity types across individuals of the same age. Especially, in the activity type sitting it is impossible to blame the accelerometer because the accelerometer shows zero movement across individuals. Therefore, I have always been surprised to see that there are people who try to estimate MET values in sedentary activity types. There is no form of machine learning that can address this problem because this is a matter of measurement construct and not a problem of classification. IN conclusion, I think it is best to stick with cut-points because they at least have some informative value: higher is more movement of the accelerometer. This may not always be directly related to energy expenditure of the person as a whole, which warrants careful interpretation of acceleration data as proxy for energy expenditure. My personal view would be to stop attempting to say anything about energy expenditure with accelerometer data and use acceleration itself as the ground truth for physical activity, e.g. cut-points thresholds informed by acceleration values across activity types rather than informed by acceleration values across energy expenditure levels.

>
> 3- Sedentary time: Is there any function in GGIR especialized in detecting sedentary time??

>>> Answer: Not yet, but for the time being you could use argument ilevels to derive time spent below a certain threshold as a crude estimate of total time in sedentary behaviour

On 29 August 2016 at 21:39, Vincent van Hees <vincent...@gmail.com> wrote:
> GGIR version 1.2-10 is now online.
>
> I have summarized the key updates here.
>
> I felt the need to change the function argument for specifying bout
> calculation again. The underlying calculations are exactly the same though.
>
> The original implementation from 2014 is still there (use bout.metric = 1 to
> get those). Earlier this year I thought the original 2014 implementation was
> inappropriate and so I added a new metric, being bout.metric 2. However,
> after thinking more about it I do not think that either one of them is truly
> superior; they are just different ways of quantifying a bout.
>
> My impression is that there is not much literature on how to count a bout in
> the presence of epoch-level data with epoch lengths shorter than 1 minute.
> So, I implemented another metric (number 3) to allow myself to compare
> various options. I documented all three metrics and added function
> g.getbout. This function should enable the user to inspect my code for bout
> calculation, test it isolated from the rest of the package, and help
> identify what metric for calculating bouts is most sensible.
>
> The challenge with designing a bout metric is that we need to decide how to
> account for breaks in bouts, how to account for the natural occurrence of
> values below or above a threshold because of the Gaussian nature of the
> data, and how to account for beliefs about what constitutes a
> physiologically meaningful bout of activity or inactivity: Do we allow
> someone to take a 10 second break? and how about a 1 minute break? Should
> the length of the maximum break length be proportional to the duration of
> the bout? Can there be activity bouts within a very long inactivity bout?
>
> If anyone knows literature investigating this issue then I would appreciate
> hearing from you. If new bout metrics are to be added in the future then I
> will just number them 4, 5, ... So, in that way reproducibility of original
> calculations should be preserved regardless of whether we like them.
>
> Thanks,
>
> Vincent
